title: Architecture Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance, and ADRs
author: Ava Patel
body:
Summary
-------
This document consolidates Redwood Inference's architecture and engineering standards across API design, coding practices, infrastructure, model-serving, observability, performance targets, and the ADR (Architecture Decision Record) process. Its goal is to provide a single, opinionated reference teams can use when designing, reviewing, and operating services that participate in the Redwood platform.

Scope
-----
Applies to: all services and libraries maintained by Redwood Inference that are customer-facing or run inference workloads, including: Redwood API, serving runtime components, Dedicated control plane components, Console, SDKs, and operational tooling.

Principles
----------
- Developer ergonomics: APIs and patterns should make the common path easy; prefer explicitness over cleverness.
- Production-first: prioritize observability, reliability, and cost in design choices.
- Consistency: common libraries and patterns reduce cognitive load and enable centralized tooling (linting, IaC modules, dashboards).
- Backwards compatible evolution: follow semantic versioning and staged rollouts for changes that affect clients.
- Security and compliance by default: treat data classification and least privilege as mandatory constraints.

1) API Standards
----------------
Intro: All public and internal HTTP/GRPC APIs must adhere to the company API standard to ensure discoverability, stable evolution, and consistent error/monitoring behavior.

Must-haves:
- Versioning: Major version in the URL or host (example: /v1/) for breaking changes; semantic versioning for SDKs and server components.
- Contracts: Use OpenAPI (REST) or proto files (gRPC) stored in the central spec repo. Specs are authoritative; generate clients from them.
- Pagination: use cursor-based pagination for lists with stable cursors.
- Idempotency: write operations must accept idempotency keys where reasonable.
- Errors:  follow the standard error envelope: { code: string, message: string, details?: object }. Map HTTP codes consistently (400s for client, 500s for server).
- Rate limiting: return 429 with Retry-After header for client-side limits; include quota codes in response headers for billing/limits telemetry.
- Authentication: JWT via Authorization header for internal services; API keys for external customers. Support mTLS between internal services where required.

Guidelines:
- Use HATEOAS links sparingly; favor explicit documented endpoints.
- Prefer JSON schema for request/response validation in OpenAPI.
- Include example requests/responses in the spec and automation to surface breaking changes in PRs.

2) Coding Standards
-------------------
Intro: Maintainable, testable code is a must. The objective is consistent style, minimal technical debt, and automated guardrails.

General rules:
- Languages: Python for orchestration and infra automation; Go for high-throughput services; TypeScript for frontend and Console backend. Exceptions require approval.
- Formatting & linting: enforce with CI (black/isort/ruff for Python, gofmt/golangci-lint for Go, eslint/prettier for TypeScript).
- Complexity limits: single function should not exceed ~80 lines without refactor; cyclomatic complexity thresholds enforced by CI.
- Tests: unit tests for all modules; integration tests for cross-service contracts; regression tests for model output where applicable.  Test coverage target: 70% per-package (guideline, not absolute).
- PRs: small, focused changes; include a short description, test plan, and checklist (security, perf, observability).

Secure coding:
- Use secrets manager integrations (KMS + HashiCorp Vault) — never commit secrets.
- Validate inputs and use typed interfaces at service boundaries.

3) Infrastructure & IaC Standards
--------------------------------
Intro: Infrastructure must be reproducible, peer-reviewed, and auditable.

Rules:
- IaC: Terraform for cloud infra modules; keep small, reusable modules in shared registry. State: remote S3/GCS with locking.
- Environments: support three canonical environments: dev, staging, prod. All config differences must be explicit via variables or 12-factor env config.
- Networking: VPCs with service-focused subnets; private subnets for GPUs and databases. Ingress via API gateway with WAF rules.
- Secrets & keys: rotate keys on a 90-day schedule; use KMS + HSM for customer-sensitive keys.
- Observability hooks: every provisioned service must include an observability module (metrics, logs forwarding, distributed tracing).

Minimal Terraform module table:
| Module name | Purpose | Owner | Required outputs |
|-------------|---------|-------|------------------|
| redwood-vpc | Network foundation | infra-team | vpc_id, subnet_ids |
| gpu-pool | Dedicated GPU autoscaling | infra-gpu | cluster_id, node_group |
| service-ecs | Run services | platform-team | service_name, target_group |

4) Model-serving Standards
--------------------------
Intro: Model-serving covers the runtime and orchestration of weights, caching, batching, quantization, and routes between model variants. The goal is repeatable quality and predictable economics.

Rules:
- Model provenance: every model must have a model manifest (JSON) listing architecture, tokenizer, quantization profile, training dataset id(s), and a content-approval tag.
- Versioning & pinning: support explicit model version pinning per-route and runtime. Rolling major model upgrades require regression evaluations and canary rollouts.
- Quantization: ship quantization profiles as part of model artifacts. Use standardized formats (e.g., ONNX + quant config) and record expected perf/quality tradeoffs.
- Caching & batching: services must surface configuration for prefix caching and batching policies; defaults follow conservative latency-first values.
- Fallbacks: route policy must support automatic fallback to compatible variant (e.g., 16-bit to 8-bit) with circuit-breaker and error-budget awareness.

Operational checks before production model rollout:
1. Regression evals against golden prompt set with acceptance thresholds.
2. Perf benchmarks (p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec) on representative hardware.
3. Capacity planning runbook updated with projected RPS and token-rate.

5) Observability Standards
-------------------------
Intro: Observability is required for all services. Standard metrics and tracing conventions enable cross-team debugging and SLO measurement.

Metrics:
- Libraries: use OpenTelemetry metrics and traces.
- Naming: metric.name should be dotted with service prefix (redwood.<service>.<metric>). Use _total, _seconds, _bytes suffix conventions.
- Required metrics: request_count (labels: route, method, status), request_latency_seconds_bucket (histogram), error_count, token_consumption_total (for inference services), queue_depth, batch_size_distribution.
- Tagging: include deployment_id, region, model_version, and route in labels where relevant.

Tracing & Logs:
- Trace all long-running requests (>50ms) and inference spans for model execution. Pass W3C traceparent headers across services.
- Logs: structured JSON logs; include correlation IDs and severity. Avoid PII in logs.

Dashboards & Alerts:
- Create a per-service dashboard showing: latency percentiles, error rate, traffic, token rate, and cost signals (tokens/sec * unit_cost).
- Alerts: SLO burn alerts, high error-rate (>= 1% for 10 minutes), sudden latency spikes (p99 increases 2x over baseline), queue/backlog > threshold. Alert routing by severity to oncall + slack channel.

6) Performance Standards & SLOs
-----------------------------
SLOs (default for public inference endpoints):
- Availability: 99.9% (monthly) for hosted API control plane endpoints.
- Latency targets (tail-aware): p50 <= 50ms, p95 <= 200ms, p99 <= 500ms for short prompts (<= 64 tokens) on supported hardware profiles. Longer prompts documented per-route.
- Token throughput: document expected tokens/sec per hardware SKU.

Benchmarking playbook (short):
1. Use standard benchmark harness (see eval-harness) with representative prompt sets.
2. Warm caches/kvs to steady state.
3. Run multi-load profiles (light, nominal, burst). Capture latency percentiles, CPU/GPU utilization, memory, and kernel-level metrics.
4. Record results in the performance registry and attach to release.

7) ADR (Architecture Decision Record) Process
-------------------------------------------
Purpose: Record architectural decisions with context, consequences, and ownership so future contributors can understand tradeoffs.

Format (required fields):
- title (short)
- date
- status (proposed | accepted | deprecated)
- context (what problem)
- decision (what we chose)
- consequences (operational and technical)
- alternatives considered
- owner

Process:
1. Draft ADR as markdown in the central ADRs repo under a new file prefixed with YYYY-MM-DD-title.md.
2. Attach related benchmarks/specs.
3. Request review from impacted teams (send to #arch-review).
4. After at least two reviewers approve and owner sign-off, mark ADR as accepted and link from this central standards doc.

Example ADR summary:
- title: Standardize model manifest format
- date: 2026-06-15
- status: accepted
- decision: adopt JSON manifest v1 with fields {id, version, tokenizer, quant_profile, provenance, approved_by}
- consequences: easier automated onboarding, consistent QA; requires updates to model onboarding tooling.

Governance & Ownership
----------------------
- Standards steward: Architecture & Standards working group (rotating leads from Platform, Serving Runtime, and Infra).
- Review gates: Breaking API changes and infra/network changes require an ADR and cross-team sign-off.
- Exceptions: documented as ADRs with explicit mitigation and timebox.

Adoption Checklist (for new services)
------------------------------------
1. API spec committed to central repo (OpenAPI/proto).
2. CI enforces formatting/linting and runs unit/integration tests.
3. Terraform module usage for infra; review by infra team.
4. Observability module integrated and dashboard scaffold created.
5. Performance/regression tests run and artifacts attached.
6. ADRs created for any non-conformant or risky decisions.

Appendices
---------
A. Standard error envelope example
{
  "code": "invalid_request",
  "message": "Prompt exceeds maximum allowed token length",
  "details": { "max_tokens": 2048 }
}

B. Quick reference for metric names
- redwood.<service>.request_count_total
- redwood.<service>.request_latency_seconds_bucket
- redwood.inference.token_consumption_total

C. Helpful links
- ADR repo: /repos/arch/adrs
- OpenAPI central specs: /repos/specs/openapi
- IaC registry: /repos/infra/modules
- Eval harness: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/eval-harness

If you have questions or want to propose an update, please file a PR against this page or raise a ticket in #arch-standards.
